analysis.investment_thesis: Maharashtra Scooters is a Bajaj-group holding company trading at a steep 55% discount to book value (P/B 0.45), with a near-zero debt balance sheet and consistent dividend payouts — but the abysmal ROE of 0.69% and declining revenue make it unsuitable as a core holding in my framework. This is a structural NAV discount play, not the steady operating compounder I seek.
key_strengths: Fortress balance sheet: effectively zero debt (equity INR 30,863 Cr vs assets INR 34,588 Cr), D/E near zero — passes my most critical test
Trading at 55% discount to book value (P/B 0.45) with INR 30,863 Cr equity vs INR 15,007 Cr market cap — deep value for a patient holder
Bajaj group parentage under Bajaj Holdings — strong governance pedigree, consistent dividend payouts (financing CF -INR 193 Cr in FY25 signals real earnings)
key_risks: ROE of 0.69% and ROCE of 0.55% are structurally catastrophic — far below my 15% floor; this is inherent to bloated holding company balance sheets
P/E of 41.8x is expensive for a business with -1.9% revenue CAGR and EBITDA contracting at -9.6% CAGR — you are paying growth multiples for a declining business
Revenue fell from INR 222 Cr (FY24) to INR 183 Cr (FY25) — a 17.6% single-year drop; not the stable, predictable cash generation I require
red_flags: ROE 0.69% — fails my 15% minimum by a factor of 20x
P/E 41.8x on declining revenue and contracting EBITDA is a dangerous combination
Not an operating business — I do not build portfolios around passive holding companies with no pricing power or consumer franchise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Maharashtra Scooters is not a scooter company — it is a Bajaj-group investment vehicle that holds a large portfolio of securities, functioning as a listed closed-end fund at a steep discount to NAV. The balance sheet tells the real story: INR 34,588 Cr in assets backed almost entirely by INR 30,863 Cr in equity, with negligible liabilities. The stock at INR 15,007 Cr market cap implies you are buying this portfolio for 49 paise on the rupee. For a special-situation or deep-value investor, this NAV discount is the entire thesis. The net profit growth of 14.5% CAGR (INR 143 Cr to INR 214 Cr) and four consecutive years of positive operating cash flow reinforce that the underlying portfolio is generating real returns.

However, this business fails almost every operational metric I care about. ROE of 0.69% is not a minor shortfall — it signals that INR 30,863 Cr of capital earns just INR 214 Cr in profits; an operating business with these returns would be liquidated. Revenue is declining (-1.9% 3-year CAGR), EBITDA is contracting sharply, and a P/E of 41.8x prices in optimism that the financials do not justify. I built DMart on the principle that great businesses earn 18-22% on capital, year after year, in sectors I understand. A passive holding company with sub-1% ROE, no consumer franchise, and no pricing power is not something I would anchor my capital in — regardless of the NAV discount. Existing holders may stay for the discount to unwind; I would not initiate.
